title: Code to Learn with Generative AI: A Theoretically Grounded Framework for Artifact Construction in Upper-Secondary Education
content: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can now write working code from a few sentences of natural language, and upper-secondary students have started to use it for exactly that. The dominant policy response has been to ask when and how much AI should be allowed, while the AI-literacy literature asks what students should understand about these systems. Neither question tells a teacher how to design a lesson in which students build software with AI and actually learn the subject the software is about. This gap matters because recent field evidence shows that learners who lean on unguarded AI perform well while they have access to it and then underperform once it is withdrawn. We address the gap with a conceptual framework, Code-to-Learn with Generative AI (CtL-GenAI), aimed at students aged roughly 15 to 18. The framework rests on a deliberate synthesis of constructionism, cognitive load theory, self-regulated learning, the ICAP model of cognitive engagement, and sociocultural accounts of scaffolding. Its organising claim is simple to state and consequential in practice: the AI writes the code, but the student writes the model. We translate this claim into six design principles, each traced to its theoretical source, and into a fivephase instructional cycle (Frame, Specify, Co-construct, Validate, Reflect and Share). Two worked scenarios, an environmental monitoring application and an interactive simulation of Newtonian mechanics, illustrate how the framework discriminates productive from unproductive uses of AI. We close with boundary conditions, assessment implications, and a set of testable propositions intended to seed empirical work.
